articles.title: Court blocks DHS policy limiting international student training opportunities
articles.summary: A federal judge ruled that higher education groups challenging new Department of Homeland Security limits on the Curricular Practical Training (CPT) program are likely to succeed. As a result, the court blocked the DHS policy restricting international student training opportunities.
articles.insight:
This ruling temporarily halts U.S. restrictions on Curricular Practical Training, potentially preserving post-study work access for international students—a key factor in destination choice—though broader visa policy uncertainty and competing global pathways mean demand shifts remain contingent on enforcement and appeals.  
Admissions teams should track the legal outcome’s finality, DHS’s next steps, and comparative CPT/OPT clarity versus UK/Australia/NZ graduate work rights, while ensuring recruitment messaging accurately reflects current U.S. training eligibility without overpromising pending policy resolution.

articles.title: International students decrease, Australian universities massively lay off students
articles.summary: The University of Melbourne cut nearly 180 employees due to a decline in international student numbers and five consecutive years of insufficient revenue. Other Australian universities are implementing similar staff reductions.
articles.insight:
This news signals potential softening in Australia’s appeal to international students, possibly reflecting broader shifts in source market preferences, visa policy perceptions, or value-for-money calculations—though it may also stem from institution-specific financial management rather than systemic demand decline.  
Admissions teams should monitor Australian competitor enrolment data, visa refusal trends, and student sentiment surveys from key markets like India and China, while assessing whether their own value propositions align with evolving expectations around post-study work rights and cost-of-living transparency.

articles.title: New Enamed gets closer to exams applied in the USA and other countries
articles.summary: Brazil’s Enamed (National Medical Training Assessment Examination) has been made mandatory for new doctors’ registration following a law sanctioned by President Lula in early November 2026. This change aligns Brazil with other countries that require standardized assessments to verify minimum medical training standards before licensure.
articles.insight:
Brazil’s new mandatory Enamed exam may gradually shift some Latin American students—particularly those previously considering domestic medical training—toward international programs in the USA, UK, Australia, or New Zealand, though demand impacts remain uncertain given local capacity, cost barriers, and existing bilateral recognition pathways.  
Admissions teams should track Enamed pass rates, Brazilian Ministry of Education policy updates, and student survey data on post-Enamed intentions—noting that any meaningful enrollment uptick would likely unfold over 2–3 years and require targeted outreach to pre-med and early-med cohorts.

articles.title: China Proposes Tougher Rules to Curb Skills Certification Fraud
articles.url: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019293/China Proposes Tougher Rules to Curb Skills Certification Fraud
articles.summary: China has introduced a draft regulation that would establish the first dedicated rules for vocational skills certifications. The draft prohibits certification institutions from issuing certificates without conducting proper assessments.
articles.insight:
This regulatory move signals China’s intensified focus on vocational education quality and credential integrity, which may gradually shift domestic perceptions of overseas academic versus vocational pathways—though direct impacts on international student demand remain uncertain and likely medium- to long-term.  
Admissions teams should monitor Chinese provincial education authorities’ implementation timelines and any resulting shifts in vocational training enrolment or outbound mobility patterns, particularly among non-degree-seeking students, while continuing to assess how this aligns with broader national upskilling priorities.

articles.title: UK business schools report declining international enrolments and predict the downturn will persist through 2027
articles.summary: UK business schools reported declining international enrolments in the 2026 Chartered Association of Business Schools Annual Membership Survey and anticipate the downturn will continue through 2027. This trend is attributed primarily to current and forthcoming UK government policies that are complicating overseas recruitment and deterring some international students.
articles.insight:
UK business schools’ reported enrolment decline—tied to restrictive UK immigration policies—may signal softening demand from key source markets, though it remains unclear whether this reflects broader global shifts or UK-specific policy impacts.  
Admissions teams should monitor application trends from overlapping origin regions (e.g., India, Nigeria, China), track competitor messaging on visa stability, and assess whether peer institutions are adjusting recruitment tactics in response to perceived UK policy risk.

articles.title: Number of Hong Kong students in US down 27% over past 10 years
articles.summary: The number of international students from Hong Kong studying in the United States has declined by nearly 27 percent over the past decade. In the most recent school year, however, there was a slight 0.5 percent year-on-year increase, driven primarily by a 4.1 percent rise in undergraduate enrollment.
articles.insight:
The 27% decade-long decline in Hong Kong students in the US likely reflects shifting geopolitical perceptions, tightened visa scrutiny, and growing competition from other English-speaking destinations—but causality remains complex and may also involve demographic and economic factors.  
Admissions teams should monitor Hong Kong-specific application trends, visa processing times, and sentiment shifts via local education fairs and agent feedback, while assessing whether recent modest US undergraduate growth signals a potential inflection point worth targeted outreach.

articles.title: Brazil has the fourth worst proficiency in English in Latin America, says survey
articles.summary: Brazil ranks fourth lowest in English proficiency among Latin American countries, according to the EF English Proficiency Index 2026 survey conducted by Education First. The survey was published on November 20, 2026, at 2:10 pm.
articles.insight:
Brazil’s low English proficiency ranking may indirectly influence demand for pre-sessional and pathway programs in English-speaking countries, though actual enrollment shifts depend more on economic conditions, visa policies, and institutional support than proficiency scores alone.  
Admissions teams should monitor Brazilian applicants’ uptake of English preparation options, IELTS/TOEFL waiver trends, and partnerships with local language providers—while avoiding assumptions that proficiency metrics alone predict application volume or conversion rates.

articles.title: Indonesia, Thailand have most Southeast Asian universities in top 100 of global science ranking
articles.summary: Indonesia and Thailand have the most Southeast Asian universities in the top 100 of a newly released global interdisciplinary science ranking. Indonesia has four universities in the top 100, while Thailand has three.
articles.insight:
This ranking signals growing regional academic confidence in Indonesia and Thailand, which may gradually influence student aspirations—though it’s unclear whether stronger domestic options will reduce outbound mobility or instead raise overall demand for high-quality education globally.  
Admissions teams should monitor enrolment trends from these countries, especially in STEM fields, and assess whether partnerships with top-ranked universities there could enhance recruitment credibility or pathway opportunities.

articles.title: US study abroad ROI under threat? Microsoft, Adobe PERM suspensions and IBM sponsorship cuts hit Indian STEM graduates; what students planning a Master’s degree need to know
articles.summary: US technology companies including Microsoft, Adobe, and IBM are scaling back or suspending H-1B and Green Card sponsorship for international employees, particularly affecting Indian STEM graduates pursuing Master’s degrees in the US. These changes—driven by PERM restrictions, heightened immigration scrutiny, and declining international student enrollment—are increasing uncertainty around post-study employment and permanent residency prospects for Fall 2027 applicants.
articles.insight:
This news may dampen perceived US ROI for Indian STEM Master’s applicants, potentially shifting demand toward the UK, Australia, and New Zealand—though actual enrollment impacts depend on broader factors like visa policy stability and alternative job market access.  
Admissions teams should track Indian student application trends by destination and program type over the next 6–12 months, while reviewing messaging around career outcomes, employer partnerships, and post-study work pathways to ensure transparency and responsiveness.
